```{r setup}
library(controlcompR)
```

Robust control asks whether a controller keeps the loop stable, and
performing well, for every plant in a set, not just for the nominal model.
For every method below the article states the uncertainty model, the
guarantee, the algorithm and the limits. Nominal stability (the design
model) and robust stability (the whole set) are different claims; a
controller that works on a few sampled plants has not been shown to be
robust.

## Unstructured uncertainty and the small-gain theorem

Three standard families describe the true plant \(G_\Delta\) with a stable
perturbation \(\|\Delta\|_\infty \le 1\) and a frequency weight \(W\):

| family | true plant | robust stability iff |
|---|---|---|
| multiplicative output | \((I + W\Delta) G\) | \(\|T W\|_\infty < 1\) |
| multiplicative input | \(G (I + W\Delta)\) | \(\|T_i W\|_\infty < 1\) |
| additive | \(G + W \Delta\) | \(\|K S W\|_\infty < 1\) |

with \(S = (I + GK)^{-1}\), \(T = GKS\) and \(T_i = KG(I + KG)^{-1}\).
These conditions are necessary and sufficient for unstructured complex
perturbations (given nominal internal stability and the same number of
unstable poles for all plants); they can be conservative for structured or
real parametric uncertainty.

A weight that is small at low frequency and grows past one at high
frequency says: the model is accurate to 10 percent at low frequency and
unreliable (up to 200 percent error) at high frequency:

```{r}
G <- ctrl_tf(1, c(1, 1))
W <- ctrl_tf(c(0.2, 0.1), c(0.1, 1))   # 0.1 at DC, 2 at high frequency
for (k in c(2, 5, 20)) {
  rs <- ctrl_robust_stability(G, ctrl_tf(k, 1), W)
  cat("K =", k, ": peak", signif(rs$peak, 3), "robustly stable:",
      rs$robustly_stable, "\n")
}
```

The returned `margin = 1 / peak` is the largest scaling of the
uncertainty that the loop tolerates. The yes or no answer is decided on
`upper_bound`, the certified upper bound of the H-infinity norm
computation, not on its estimate.

## Robust performance

Robust stability says nothing about how well the perturbed loops perform.
With a performance weight \(W_p\) on the sensitivity, the requirement
\(\|W_p S_p\|_\infty < 1\) for every plant \((I + W_u\Delta)G\) holds
when
\[
\sup_\omega \; |W_p|\,\bar\sigma(S) + |W_u|\,\bar\sigma(T) < 1 ,
\]
which is exact for SISO loops and sufficient (possibly conservative) for
MIMO loops with scalar weights. A PI controller with integral action is
needed for the performance weight below, which demands small sensitivity
at low frequency:

```{r}
Wp <- ctrl_tf(c(0.5, 0.5), c(1, 0.01))   # |S| below 2 % at low frequency
Wu <- ctrl_tf(c(0.5, 0.1), c(0.25, 1))  # 10 % at DC, 200 % at high frequency
for (kp in c(0.5, 1, 8)) {
  K <- ctrl_tf(c(kp, 1), c(1, 0))
  rp <- ctrl_robust_performance(G, K, Wp, Wu)
  cat("kp =", kp, ": peak", signif(rp$peak, 3),
      " robust performance:", rp$robust_performance,
      " robust stability:", rp$robust_stability, "\n")
}
```

The `curve` element holds the frequency-wise test value for plotting. The
peak is sampled on a dense grid that includes zero and infinite frequency,
with local refinement, so it is a lower bound on the supremum. The
`certified` flag adds a rigorous check: it is `TRUE` when the upper bound
\(\|W_p S\|_\infty + \|W_u T\|_\infty\) from certified norm computations
(`upper_bound`) is also below one. A gain that is too low misses
the performance target, a gain that is too high loses robust stability
itself, and the middle gain meets both.

## Generalized plants

Optimal synthesis works with a generalized plant `P` with exogenous inputs
`w` (disturbances, noise, references), controls `u`, performance outputs
`z` and measurements `y`. `ctrl_lft()` closes the loop `u = K y`:

```{r}
A <- matrix(c(0, 1, 0, 0), 2, byrow = TRUE)
# w = (process noise on both states, sensor noise), u = force
# z = (position, control effort), y = noisy position
P <- ctrl_ss(A, cbind(diag(2), 0, c(0, 1)),
             rbind(c(1, 0), c(0, 0), c(1, 0)),
             rbind(c(0, 0, 0, 0), c(0, 0, 0, 1), c(0, 0, 1, 0)))
```

`ctrl_plant_partition()` splits the generalized plant into the blocks
used by the synthesis formulas, given the numbers of measurements and
controls (the last outputs and inputs). The rank conditions on
\(D_{12}\) and \(D_{21}\) are checked relative to each block's own size,
so they do not depend on the units of `z`, `u`, `w` or `y`:

```{r}
pp <- ctrl_plant_partition(P, nmeas = 1, ncon = 1)
pp$D12
pp$D21
```

## H2 synthesis

`ctrl_h2syn()` minimizes \(\|T_{zw}\|_2\), the root-mean-square response of
`z` to unit white noise `w`. The solution uses two Riccati equations, one
for the regulator and one for the filter (Zhou, Doyle and Glover, Theorem
14.7). It needs \(D_{11} = 0\), \(D_{12}\) of full column rank, \(D_{21}\) of
full row rank, \((A, B_2)\) stabilizable and \((C_2, A)\) detectable; all
are checked. LQG is the special case above:

```{r}
h2 <- ctrl_h2syn(P, nmeas = 1, ncon = 1)
h2
```

## H-infinity synthesis (experimental)

`ctrl_hinfsyn()` finds a controller with \(\|T_{zw}\|_\infty < \gamma\),
bounding the worst-case energy gain from `w` to `z`, and searches the
smallest \(\gamma\) by bisection. The algorithm is the two-Riccati
solution of Glover and Doyle (1988) after normalizing \(D_{12}\) and
\(D_{21}\) with orthogonal transformations (which do not change the norm).
A level \(\gamma\) is feasible when both Riccati equations have
stabilizing solutions \(X_\infty, Y_\infty \succeq 0\) and
\(\rho(X_\infty Y_\infty) < \gamma^2\).

**Every controller is certified independently**: the closed loop must be
internally stable and its H-infinity norm, computed by a different
algorithm (Bruinsma-Steinbuch), must have an upper bound below
\(\gamma\). Otherwise the function stops with an error. When the H2
optimal controller already gives a zero closed-loop norm, that attained
optimum is returned with `gamma = 0` (no positive bracket exists).

```{r}
hinf <- ctrl_hinfsyn(P, nmeas = 1, ncon = 1)
hinf
c(h2_controller = ctrl_norm(h2$closed_loop, "inf"),
  hinf_controller = hinf$norm)
c(h2_controller = ctrl_norm(h2$closed_loop, "2"),
  hinf_controller = ctrl_norm(hinf$closed_loop, "2"))
```

Each controller is best in its own norm: the H-infinity design lowers the
worst-case gain at the price of a much larger H2 norm. The bisection log shows the
search:

```{r}
tail(hinf$history)
```

**Scope.** Continuous time only and \(D_{11} = 0\). Discrete time
synthesis, general \(D_{11}\), structured singular values (mu) and
mu-synthesis are not implemented; the package refuses these problems
rather than approximating them.

## Mixed-sensitivity design

Shaping \(S\), \(KS\) and \(T\) with weights is the classical way to state
H-infinity design goals: small sensitivity at low frequency (tracking and
disturbance rejection), limited control effort, small complementary
sensitivity at high frequency (noise and robustness). `ctrl_augw()` builds
the generalized plant; with the \(D_{11} = 0\) restriction the
sensitivity weight `W1` must be strictly proper:

```{r}
G <- ctrl_tf(1, c(1, 3, 2))
W1 <- ctrl_tf(1, c(1, 0.01))   # integral-like: demands small S at low frequency
P_ms <- ctrl_augw(G, W1 = W1, W2 = 0.1)
syn <- ctrl_hinfsyn(P_ms, nmeas = 1, ncon = 1)
syn$gamma
K <- syn$K
L <- ctrl_series(K, G)
S <- ctrl_feedback(1, L)
w <- 10^seq(-3, 2, length.out = 200)
df <- data.frame(
  w = rep(w, 2),
  magnitude = c(Mod(ctrl_freqresp(S, w)$response[1, 1, ]),
                syn$gamma / Mod(ctrl_freqresp(W1, w)$response[1, 1, ])),
  curve = rep(c("|S|", "gamma / |W1|"), each = length(w)))
ggplot2::ggplot(df, ggplot2::aes(w, magnitude, color = curve)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line() + ggplot2::scale_x_log10() + ggplot2::scale_y_log10() +
  ggplot2::theme_bw()
```

The sensitivity stays below \(\gamma / |W_1|\) at all frequencies, as the
norm bound guarantees. Plant poles on the imaginary axis (integrators)
are not driven by `w` in this setup and make the Riccati equations
singular; shift them slightly into the left half plane for the design and
check the controller on the true plant.

## Margins as robustness measures

Gain, phase and disk margins (see the frequency response article) are
robustness measures for single loops. The disk margin is the more
reliable of them because it covers simultaneous gain and phase changes:

```{r}
ctrl_disk_margin(L)
```
